title: The Declaration of Independence Details “Repeated Injuries” Inflicted by British Monarchy, Trump Has Executed a Similar Playbook
summary: Our country was founded around our independence from a king — Trump’s actions fly in the face of these principals.

# The Declaration of Independence Details “Repeated Injuries” Inflicted by British Monarchy, Trump Has Executed a Similar Playbook


The Founding Fathers declared independence from despotism 250 years ago. Today we’re fighting against similar abuses of power from a wannabe king.


[Johanna Silver](https://www.aclu.org/bios/johanna-silver-2) ,
she/her/hers


,
ACLU


**Share This Page**


July 2, 2026


Delegates from across the original 13 colonies signed the Declaration of Independence 250 years ago on July 4, 1776 detailing the abuses of the King of England that led to their fight for sovereignty. Their condemnation feels all too familiar today.


The Declaration of Independence proclaimed the country’s original 13 colonies separate from the rule of the British monarchy. It also established people’s “unalienable rights” and emphasized the government’s role of protecting the rights of the governed, helping to form the principles and framework for the new country.


The document details King George III’s “repeated injuries and usurpations,” that led to the colonies’ fight for sovereignty. That list reveals parallels between the cruelty of King George III and the current abuses of President Donald Trump. Throughout his second term, President Trump has[repeatedly committed civil rights offenses](https://www.aclu.org/news/civil-liberties/one-year-in-defending-the-constitution-under-a-second-trump-administration) that fly in the face of the promises outlined by the Founding Fathers. From the start, our country has championed a rule of law that supports the rights of the governed and not the whims of a despot — 250 years later, we’re still proclaiming[No Kings](https://www.nokings.org/) .


Below, learn more about some of the monarchical offenses outlined in the Declaration of Independence, how Trump’s administration has taken similar offending actions, and how the ACLU is fighting back to protect our rights.


Credit: Andrea Izzotti/ Shutterstock


> *“He has dissolved Representative Houses repeatedly, for opposing with manly firmness his invasions on the rights of the people.”*


The Trump administration has repeatedly tried to sideline Congress and undermine its ability to act as a check on executive power. For example, the Trump administration has repeatedly ignored[federal spending laws](https://www.aclu.org/news/civil-liberties/trumps-attempt-to-unilaterally-control-state-and-local-funding-is-dangerous-dumb-and-undemocratic) and eliminated and hollowed out statutorily mandated agencies like the[Department of Education](https://www.aclu.org/news/racial-justice/trumps-attack-on-the-department-of-education-explained) , USAID, and[civil rights enforcement offices](https://www.aclu.org/news/racial-justice/trumps-attempt-to-roll-back-key-civil-rights-enforcement-tool) . The Trump administration also undermines Congress by ignoring or attacking oversight, such as by stonewalling[congressional oversight visits](https://www.aclu.org/news/immigrants-rights/hundreds-at-delaney-hall-join-detained-people-across-country-in-hunger-strike-against-inhumane-conditions) to immigration detention centers.


> *“He has endeavoured to prevent the population of these States; for that purpose obstructing the Laws for Naturalization of Foreigners; refusing to pass others to encourage their migration hither, and raising the conditions of new Appropriations of Lands.”*


President Trump has targeted immigrants’ rights since his first day back in office, principally by attempting to eliminate birthright citizenship as a constitutional guarantee. He has also weaponized federal forces to unlawfully confront and seize individuals, often without any legitimate cause. The ACLU has been a frontline force against these unlawful actions. We took the fight to protect birthright citizenship[all the way to the Supreme Court — and won](https://www.aclu.org/news/immigrants-rights/supreme-court-rules-to-protect-birthright-citizenship-in-landmark-case) — while continuing to highlight the federal government’s offenses against immigrants in and out of the courtroom.


> *“He has kept among us, in times of peace, Standing Armies without the Consent of our legislature.”*


In response to Trump’s anti-immigrant aggression, thousands of people have exercised their constitutionally-protected right to protest, including on university campuses and around our nation’s capital. Trump has deployed the National Guard and other federal agents into our country’s communities including[Washington D.C.](https://www.aclu.org/press-releases/aclu-statement-on-escalating-federal-takeover-of-d-c) and[Minnesota](https://www.aclu.org/news/immigrants-rights/i-have-no-rights-minnesota-residents-sue-trump-administration-for-racial-profiling-stops-without-suspicion-and-warrantless-arrests) , in an attempt to silence their dissent through intimidation. But the ACLU has been working to make sure that individuals[know their rights](https://www.aclu.org/know-your-rights/encountering-law-enforcement-and-military-troops) when they encounter or are confronted by law enforcement and federal agents. No one should be targeted, arrested, or detained for exercising their First Amendment rights.


> “ *He has affected to render the Military independent of and superior to the Civil Power.”*


Trump has used the[military to illegally declare war.](https://www.aclu.org/news/civil-liberties/your-questions-answered-can-congress-stop-president-trumps-illegal-war-against-iran) On February 28, 2026, the president started bombing Iran and announced that we were going to war, despite this power belonging solely to Congress to initiate. As bipartisan opposition grows in Congress, the[ACLU continues to urge members](https://action.aclu.org/send-message/war-on-iran) to use their power of the purse and refuse further funding of this unconstitutional war.

### Daves v. Mosley


Section 131 of the newly enacted Enhance Law Enforcement Integrity Act gives Coloradans a cause of action to seek damages or equitable relief when state or local police officers violate the Colorado Constitution. In 2022, Christopher Mosley sued Officer Brendan Daves for conducting a warrantless search of his car, which Daves argued was lawful under the federal protective sweep doctrine. After Mosley prevailed at trial and the court of appeals affirmed, Daves appealed to the Colorado Supreme Court. The ACLU’s State Supreme Court Initiative and the ACLU of Colorado filed an amicus brief agreeing with Mosley’s argument that Daves has misapprehended the federal doctrine whilst focusing on a separate point: the Court’s interpretation of Section 131 is not bound by federal law.


**Status:** Ongoing

### ACLU Celebrates the Legacy of Dolores Huerta


NEW YORK – The American Civil Liberties Union celebrates the legacy of Dolores Huerta, who passed away today at the age of 96. Huerta was one of the most influential workers’ rights leaders of the 20th century. Anthony D. Romero, ACLU executive director, had the following reaction to today’s news: “Dolores Huerta spent her life challenging injustice in every form – fighting for workers’ rights, women’s rights, immigrants’ rights, and so much more. Her bravery, perseverance, and compassion changed this country for the better. “As co-founder of the United Farm Workers Union, she successfully organized farmworker walkouts and consumer boycotts to demand better working conditions for Latino farmworkers. Today, millions of workers enjoy the protections that Ms. Huerta, and thousands of others who marched and mobilized alongside her, fought so hard to win. “The ACLU was proud to honor Ms. Huerta with the ACLU’s Roger N. Baldwin Medal of Liberty in 1993, recognizing her lifetime contributions to civil rights and civil liberties. More than three decades later, her continued legacy of standing up to injustice has stood the test of time. History will remember Dolores Huerta as a modern-day trailblazer for our rights and freedoms, and the ACLU will continue the fight to protect the justice and freedoms she spent her life working to achieve.”

### People v. Taylor


In 2013, Michigan passed the Michigan Indigent Defense Commission Act (MIDCA) to ensure that indigent criminal defendants—that is, those who cannot afford to pay for counsel themselves—received constitutionally adequate counsel, paid for by the state. This case concerns whether and under what circumstances trial courts can, consistent with MIDCA, order indigent criminal defendants to pay the state back for their attorneys. The ACLU’s State Supreme Court Initiative, the ACLU of Michigan, and the Michigan State Planning Body filed an amicus brief in the Michigan Supreme Court arguing that MIDCA, properly construed, partially abrogated a different statute authorizing trial courts to assess attorney fees against indigent defendants and explaining that allowing such orders would undermine Michiganders’ right to counsel.


**Status:** Ongoing

### ACLU Voter Education Fund and ACLU of Georgia Launch $250K Campaign to Educate Georgia Voters Ahead of Midterms


ATLANTA – The ACLU of Georgia and the ACLU Voter Education Fund are spending $250,000 in select Georgia House races to inform voters that their civil rights and liberties, including voting rights and abortion, are on the ballot this November. The ACLU Voter Education Fund will send over 225,000 mail pieces to educate voters about candidates in State House Districts 48, 53, and 105. These state races include communities like Lawrenceville, Peachtree Corners, and Sandy Springs and are highly contested. The ACLU Voter Education Fund is investing in these races because the elected candidates will influence civil rights and liberties statewide for at least two years. Their decisions will affect voting rights, reproductive rights, privacy, and other fundamental liberties. On the voter guides, residents will see candidates’ responses to questions about those issues, such as whether they would vote to repeal Georgia’s six-week abortion ban or whether they will work to prevent unnecessary restrictions on early and absentee voting. “Georgia voters have a right to know the positions that the candidates take on the rights and freedoms that shape their lives,” said Christopher Bruce, deputy executive director, ACLU of Georgia. “We’re making sure voters get the information they need to understand the issues in these elections and what the candidates would do if they had the power of the Georgia House. From reproductive freedom and voting rights to safeguarding privacy and other liberties, the choices made under the Gold Dome can have a lasting impact on our communities.” While the ACLU Voter Education Fund does not endorse or oppose any candidates, the six-figure campaign will educate voters about the candidates’ positions on key civil rights issues, including abortion, birth control, marriage equality, and voting rights for Indigenous communities, through direct mail, radio ads, and digital ads.
